question: What are the three main tiers of the Nigerian health system?
explanation: Spot on! Nigeria's health system is broken into three simple levels (primary, secondary, and tertiary) to make sure healthcare reaches everyone from local villages to big cities. [learn more](GST322_U5_T4#GST322_U5_T4_h1)

question: Why is it important for nursing students to understand how healthcare is funded?

options.A: Nurses are directly responsible for collecting hospital revenue
options.B: It explains why some facilities lack basic supplies and equipment
options.C: It is required for writing national health policies
options.D: It determines the specific salary scale for health workers

explanation: You've got this! Knowing where hospital money comes from helps you make sense of the real-world shortages and everyday challenges you will see during clinical postings. [learn more](GST322_U5_T4#GST322_U5_T4_h1)

question: What is the main purpose of the Basic Health Care Provision Fund (BHCPF) in Nigeria?

options.A: To pay retirement benefits for retired federal medical doctors
options.B: To import expensive surgical equipment for private clinics
options.C: To finance basic minimum health services at the primary care level
options.D: To build specialized teaching hospitals in every state capital

explanation: Well done! The BHCPF is set up specifically to pump money into primary healthcare, ensuring everyday community needs like immunizations are covered. [learn more](GST322_U5_T4#GST322_U5_T4_h2)

question: A community health center needs funds to buy routine vaccines. Which funding source should they look to?

options.A: The Basic Health Care Provision Fund
options.B: International research grants for cancer treatment
options.C: The capital budget of a tertiary teaching hospital
options.D: Private commercial bank loans for hospital expansion

explanation: Spot on! Routine immunizations and community health needs fall right under the umbrella of the Basic Health Care Provision Fund. [learn more](GST322_U5_T4#GST322_U5_T4_h2)

question: Which level of government is mainly responsible for funding general hospitals that provide secondary care?
explanation: Great job! State ministries of health take charge of managing and funding general hospitals, which make up our secondary care tier. [learn more](GST322_U5_T4#GST322_U5_T4_h3)

question: How do general hospitals raise some of their own operational money locally?

options.A: Through direct user fees paid by patients for services and drugs
options.B: By exporting medical laboratory reagents to other countries
options.C: Through mandatory monthly levies on local business owners
options.D: By collecting property taxes from surrounding communities

explanation: Exactly right! Hospitals often generate internal cash by collecting service charges, consultation fees, and drug payments directly from patients. [learn more](GST322_U5_T4#GST322_U5_T4_h3)

question: Where does most of the money for federal teaching hospitals come from?
explanation: You nailed it! Teaching hospitals are big federal projects, so they rely heavily on the national budget to keep running. [learn more](GST322_U5_T4#GST322_U5_T4_h4)

question: Why is tertiary healthcare so much more expensive to run than primary healthcare?

options.A: It only treats wealthy patients who can afford high insurance premiums
options.B: It requires advanced technology, specialized personnel, and research facilities
options.C: It employs more administrative staff than clinical nurses and doctors
options.D: It must purchase all medications directly from international manufacturers

explanation: Spot on! Tertiary centers handle complex cases requiring high-tech equipment, ICUs, and specialists, which naturally drives up the cost. [learn more](GST322_U5_T4#GST322_U5_T4_h4)

question: What is the main goal of a health insurance scheme?

options.A: To pool financial risks and protect people from high out-of-pocket costs
options.B: To ensure that doctors receive higher salaries than other workers
options.C: To provide free luxury accommodation for all hospitalized patients
options.D: To eliminate the need for government funding in hospitals

explanation: Great thinking! Insurance pools money from many people so that when someone falls sick, they don't get completely wiped out financially by medical bills. [learn more](GST322_U5_T4#GST322_U5_T4_h5)

question: How do State Health Insurance Agencies usually differ from the federal NHIA initiative?

options.A: They only provide care for surgical emergencies in private clinics
options.B: They prohibit civil servants from accessing any form of medical care
options.C: They focus heavily on covering informal sector workers and rural dwellers in their states
options.D: They are funded exclusively by grants from foreign international banks

explanation: You're getting it! While federal schemes started with government workers, state agencies make special efforts to reach traders, artisans, and rural villagers. [learn more](GST322_U5_T4#GST322_U5_T4_h5)

question: What does an "out-of-pocket" payment mean in healthcare?

options.A: Reimbursement given to nurses for buying personal uniforms
options.B: Grants donated by foreign organizations to rural clinics
options.C: Monthly salary deductions paid automatically by the government
options.D: Direct cash payment made by patients at the point of receiving service

explanation: Spot on! Out-of-pocket means the patient is dipping straight into their own wallet to pay for drugs, tests, and consultations right there at the hospital. [learn more](GST322_U5_T4#GST322_U5_T4_h6)

question: A patient skips buying blood pressure meds because they have no cash, relying on herbs instead. What is the biggest danger of relying solely on out-of-pocket spending?

options.A: Better compliance with long-term medication schedules
options.B: Immediate financial relief and permanent cure of the hypertension
options.C: Automatic enrollment into the state health insurance scheme
options.D: Delayed care and increased risk of severe complications like stroke

explanation: Sad but true. When people have to pay cash upfront for everything, they often skip treatment, which can lead to life-threatening emergencies like strokes. [learn more](GST322_U5_T4#GST322_U5_T4_h6)

question: Which health areas are most commonly supported by international donors and NGOs in Nigeria?

options.A: Specific disease programs like HIV/AIDS, malaria, and polio
options.B: Routine administrative salaries of state commissioners of health
options.C: Importation of luxury vehicles for hospital management boards
options.D: Construction of private mansions for retired medical directors

explanation: Correct! International partners love to channel their resources into major public health campaigns and infectious disease control. [learn more](GST322_U5_T4#GST322_U5_T4_h7)

question: What is a major risk of depending too much on donor funding for national healthcare?

options.A: Private hospitals will take over all government teaching hospitals
options.B: Local healthcare workers will refuse to treat insured patients
options.C: Patients will stop paying out-of-pocket for their medications
options.D: Services may collapse when donor priorities change or funding ends

explanation: Well reasoned! External aid can be unstable. If foreign partners pack up or shift their focus, programs without local backup can easily crash. [learn more](GST322_U5_T4#GST322_U5_T4_h7)

question: Which of these is NOT a major challenge facing healthcare financing in Nigeria?

options.A: Heavy reliance on out-of-pocket payments by ordinary citizens
options.B: Excessive availability of well-managed public funds in primary centers
options.C: Inefficient resource distribution and management weaknesses
options.D: Inadequate budgetary allocations from government tiers

explanation: You got it! Primary health centers definitely do *not* have excess funds; rather, they struggle with severe underfunding and poor management. [learn more](GST322_U5_T4#GST322_U5_T4_h8)

question: How does expanding mandatory health insurance help solve healthcare financing problems?

options.A: It creates a reliable, pooled fund that reduces financial barriers for patients
options.B: It allows doctors to set their own salaries without government review
options.C: It forces international donors to double their annual monetary grants
options.D: It completely eliminates the need for primary healthcare centers

explanation: Brilliant! Mandatory insurance keeps a steady flow of money coming into hospitals while saving everyday people from sudden, crushing medical bills. [learn more](GST322_U5_T4#GST322_U5_T4_h8)
